To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

The prevalence of HIV- 1 drug resistance mutations is high in children previously exposed at birth to single- dose nevirapine, but standard genotyping is adequate for identifying children who could benefit for switching to a nevirpine-based regimen.

the prevalence of HIV drug resistance in infants exposed to sdNvp and initiating ART is high, that resistance to NRTIs was not common, that NNRTI resistance mutations were common in children less than 6–12months of age, and that NNRTI drug resistance was associated with viral failure at 12 months post randomization.

the prevalence of HIV drug resistance mutations at treatment initiation was high in HIV-infected children exposed to sdNvp and initiating lopinavir/ritonavir-based therapy, but standard genotyping is adequate for identifying children who would benefit from switching to an NNRTI-based regimen.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of antiretrovials to treat and prevent HIV infection.
the use of antiretrovials in children infected with HIV-1 and the development of antiretrovirals for use in children.
the development of novel methods for the diagnosis and treatment of HIV infection in children, and the prevention of transmission of HIV from mother to child.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the prevalence of mutations known is high in sd-NVP exposed children, supporting current recommendations for use of protease inhibitors for primary therapy in this population.

the use of sdNVP is associated with a significant increase in the rate of HIV transmission to infants, but that the use of a single dose of sdNVP for prevention of mother-to-child HIV transmission in resource-poor settings is a highly effective and cost-effective intervention.
HIV-1 drug-resistant mutations were detected in 62% in the infants less than 1 year of age and 39% in the children 1–2 years of age, who were treated with SD NVP for PMTCT.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the high prevalence of NNRTI drug resistance mutations in children who received a single-dose of nevirapine for the prevention of mother-to-child HIV transmission, and who were subsequently treated with NNRTI-based regimens, was confirmed.

HIV drug resistance mutations were detected in the majority of infants exposed to single-dosing of nevirapine, and these mutations were associated with virological failure when the children were switched from protease-inhibitor based therapy to a nonnucleoside based regimen.
the prevalence of NNRTI mutations known to compromise NNRTI-based regimens is high in sd-NVP-exposed infants, supporting current guidelines to use PI-based regimens for these children.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the prevalence of drug resistance mutations in children exposed to sdNVR is high and is associated with virologic failure in children who switch to a non-protease inhibitor-based regimen.

we need a more comprehensive approach to HIV drug resistance testing in infants and young children exposed to single dose nevirapine for prevention of vertical transmission, and that this approach should take into account the potential for the presence of minority variants.
we need to be careful when using the term “resistant virus” in children exposed to single-dosage nevirapine, as the term “resistance” has been defined in adults.
